newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Public debt seen as greatest EMU bugbear.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Public debt seen as greatest EMU bugbear.

text.p: Debt burdens are expected to be the greatest obstacle for countries trying to get their economies into shape for Europe's single currency club, a Reuters survey shows.

The poll of more than 34 economists across Europe found that only three countries -- Luxembourg, France and Britain -- were expected to meet the guidelines for debt which would help make them eligible for planned currency union.
Even Germany is expected to fall just short of the debt threshold which along with four other criteria would qualify it to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), according to the findings.
Under the Maastricht treaty, aspirant members of EMU must aim for public debt during 1997 to be less than 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
The Reuters survey found unanimity among economists expecting Luxembourg and France to meet the debt guideline.
Eighteen out of 23 also expected Britain to make it, while the other five said they expected British debt to fall just short of the criterion -- between 60 and 65 percent of GDP.
Only four out of 26 economists predicted Germany's debt to be within range, although the 22 others were unanimous in their view that Germany's public debt would be between 60 and 65 percent of GDP.
The majority of economists said they also expected Finland to be just outside the 60 percent mark.
But Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden were judged by most economists to be well wide of the 60 percent debt ratio.

Other entry criteria -- governing the public sector deficit as a ratio to GDP, low inflation and bond yield rates and membership of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) -- were being approached more easily, according to the survey.

Six out of the 15 countries -- Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden -- were shaping up to have their ratio of public sector deficit to GDP under the target three percent during 1997, the poll showed.
And every EU member except Greece would have their inflation and bond yield rates within the guidelines, according to the findings of the survey.

Despite the small number of countries meeting the debt criterion, economists pointed out that it did not spell doom for EMU, as the wording of the Maastricht treaty allows for near misses to be included.
"We believe there are greater difficulties in getting into EMU than originally anticipated," said Klaus Baader, senior European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

"(But) the Maastricht criteria are to some extent being softened by the way in which they are calculated...there are greater difficulties in reaching the type of stability pact that Germany wants," he said.
"The Maastricht criteria were built with flexibility in mind," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi in London.
"There was never an intention for the countries to hit them or be damned. There is nothing sacrosanct about them."

His view is borne out by the latest Reuters monthly EMU barometer, which shows an 82 percent likelihood of currency union going ahead on its scheduled start date of January 1, 1999, with between six and eight countries taking part.
The polls were conducted among economists and political analysts across Europe from November 11 to 15.
